name: Tetracycline stain bleaching

card.summary: Weeks of overnight tray bleaching aimed at deep tetracycline stains, which resist normal whitening.
card.note: Sensitivity and gum burns from poorly fitting trays are reported.

lead: Tetracycline stain bleaching is the use of extended peroxide bleaching, usually in custom trays worn overnight for weeks or months, to lighten the yellow, grey or brown discoloration of teeth caused by tetracycline antibiotics taken during tooth development. People use it to brighten teeth and even out their color without veneers or crowns. [1][2]

Tetracycline binds calcium and becomes incorporated into developing teeth. The stain starts as a yellow-green discoloration of the dentin visible through the enamel, fluoresces under UV light, and later oxidizes to brown. Because the stain sits in the dentin, Wikipedia says it often needs prolonged bleaching, and bonding or veneers can mask it when bleaching is insufficient. [1][2]

Several clinical studies of nightguard bleaching with 10 percent carbamide peroxide on tetracycline-stained teeth have followed participants for years. In a 2010 study, three months of nightly bleaching increased tooth lightness, which was maintained at two years. [3] In a long-term follow-up of 6 months of treatment, 60 percent of 15 surveyed participants reported no obvious shade change or only slight darkening 90 months later, and none returned to their original shade. [4]

chain: Peroxide gel in a custom tray penetrates enamel to the dentin
Stain molecules in the dentin are lightened over weeks
Lighter, more even tooth color without veneers
angle.text: Weeks of overnight tray wear lighten deep tetracycline stains that ordinary whitening cannot shift. In the published follow-ups, participants were generally satisfied with the result and some chose to retreat later.

infobox: Gels up to 6% hydrogen peroxide or 16% carbamide peroxide endorsed [1]

paras: Home bleaching uses trays holding carbamide peroxide gel worn overnight or for two to four hours a day, and Wikipedia notes that results can begin within about three days. [1] Intrinsic stains form within the tooth and cannot be cleaned off, so bleaching is the general approach, with restorations such as composite, veneers or crowns to hide them. [1][2]

Wikipedia adds that tetracycline stains often need prolonged bleaching because the bleach must reach the dentine. [1] Intracoronal (internal) bleaching, used for discolored root-canal-treated teeth, carries a risk of root resorption. [1]

Haywood, Leonard and Dickinson published a six-month nightguard bleaching study of tetracycline-stained teeth in 1997. [5] A 1999 follow-up at 54 months reported that of 12 patients surveyed, 10 (83 percent) had no obvious shade change or only slight darkening after 6 months of 10 percent carbamide peroxide, and that no one reported darkening back to the original shade. [6] A 2003 follow-up at 90 months of 21 originally enrolled participants (15 surveyed, 8 examined) found that 60 percent reported no obvious shade change or only slight darkening, improvement over baseline remained significant, and no respondent reported treatment-related sensitivity or crowns or root canals. [4]

In a 2010 Odontology study, participants wore a custom tray with 10 percent carbamide peroxide nightly for three months. Lightness rose within three months and persisted for two years, color change values were 13.74, 14.02, 12.17 and 11.81 at 3, 6, 12 and 24 months, all participants were satisfied, and three reported slight hypersensitivity. [3]

Reported effects of bleaching include sensitivity, gum irritation, uneven results and rebound toward the original shade as teeth rehydrate. [1] Poorly fitting trays are a common cause of chemical burns. [1] The US FDA endorses gels up to 6 percent hydrogen peroxide or 16 percent carbamide peroxide, and EU retail products are limited to 0.1 percent hydrogen peroxide, with up to 6 percent allowed under professional supervision. [1] Bleaching is not recommended for children under 16, during pregnancy or breastfeeding, or with untreated decay or gum disease. [1]

quick.overview:
Tetracycline staining is inside the tooth, so it tends to respond slowly to whitening. Extended overnight tray bleaching is the approach this entry covers.

Veneers or crowns are the alternative options listed in references.
quick.mechanism: Peroxide gel releases reactive species that break down pigment molecules; reference sources say tetracycline stain takes longer because bleach must reach the dentine.
quick.risks: Sensitivity, gum irritation or burns, uneven results and rebound are reported. Concentration limits are set by regulators.
